title: Onset of Quantum Chaos in Random Field Theories
body:
Onset of Quantum Chaos in Random Field Theories

Micha Berkooz, Adar Sharon, Navot Silberstein, Erez Y. Urbach

Department of Particle Physics and Astrophysics,
Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot 7610001, Israel

micha.berkooz@weizmann.ac.il

adar.sharon@weizmann.ac.il

navot.silberstein@weizmann.ac.il

erez.urbach@weizmann.ac.il

October 18, 2026

Abstract

We study the quantum Lyapunov exponent in theories with spacetime-independent disorder. We first derive self-consistency equations for the two- and four-point functions for products of models coupled by disorder at large , generalizing the equations appearing in SYK-like models. We then study families of theories in which the disorder coupling is an exactly marginal deformation, allowing us to follow from weak to strong coupling. We find interesting behaviors, including a discontinuous transition into chaos, mimicking classical KAM theory.

Contents
  1. Introduction
  2. Disorder around a nontrivial CFT
    1. The kernel structure of the four-point function
    2. The double-commutator and chaos
  3. Examples of the Onset of chaos
    1. Disordered generalized free fields
    2. Disordered minimal models
  4. Acknowledgments

Introduction

Systems with disorder are ubiquitous in nature, and display a wide range of interesting physical phenomena. Disorder can sometimes be modeled by introducing random couplings, and averaging over these random couplings can lead to simplifications which allow for exact computations, at least when the number of degrees of freedom is parametrically large. A notable example is the Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev (SYK) model, in which (nearly) conformal symmetry is restored at low energies Sachdev and Ye (1993); Kitaev (2015); Maldacena and Stanford (2016); Kitaev and Suh (2018), and such averages allow for the computation of the quantum chaos exponent . The latter is defined by the fastest growing exponential mode in the double-commutator for generic operators , over an appropriate time scale, with temperature Larkin and Ovchinnikov (1969).

The SYK model consists of free quantum mechanical fermions deformed by a relevant all-to-all spacetime-independent disordered interaction. Generalizations have appeared which consist of copies of other free theories with similar interactions Murugan et al. (2017); Fu et al. (2017); Peng (2018); Bulycheva (2018); Chang et al. (2021); Popov (2020); Gross and Rosenhaus (2017); Lian et al. (2019). In this letter we study quantum chaos in a more general setting by studying copies of a general core model (which can be a quantum field theory or a spin system), deformed by a spacetime-independent all-to-all interaction. In particular, we eventually focus on being a conformal field theory (CFT) in 0+1 or in higher dimensions, and with an exactly marginal disorder interaction. In such a setup we have better control over the space of couplings over which we are averaging, eliminating the complications of the renormalization group (RG) and without having to resort to strong coupling.

In the case where is a CFT, we will take to be a primary operator of this core CFT, and equation (1) should be interpreted in conformal perturbation theory in . We call such theories disordered CFTs; the simplest example of this setup is the SYK model itself, as a disordered free fermion theory.

We will first derive self-consistency equations for the two- and four-point functions of at leading order in for general disordered CFTs. These extend known results for disordered free theories like the SYK model Maldacena and Stanford (2016); Kitaev and Suh (2018)), and for spin systems Bray and Moore (1980). We will also discuss similar results for the double-commutator (defined in (7) below). Although these self-consistency equations are complicated, they are tractable in perturbation theory in and allow us to establish the existence of a kernel structure from which we can extract the chaos exponent , which is the rate of growth of a double commutator. The latter is given by the fastest growing eigenvector (with eigenvalue 1) of a specific integral kernel (see equation (9)), as long as this rate of growth is indeed positive Kitaev (2015); Kitaev (2015); Larkin and Ovchinnikov (1969). We will denote by the putative chaos exponent read from the diagonalization .

We will be interested in computing the chaos exponent as a function of , as it is varied from weak to strong coupling. The diagonalization of is a difficult process, which can usually be done only when conformal invariance is restored. Normally, the disorder is a relevant deformation. To compute the chaos one first flow to the IR CFT (which is equivalent to take ) and find the chaos exponent there Murugan et al. (2017). In this work we focus on cases where the averaged interacting theory is conformally invariant for all . This can be done by demanding that the disorder interaction itself be exactly marginal, in which case the theory is conformally invariant for every realization of the couplings, and the space of ’s forms a conformal manifold 1. The disorder average is then simply a non-uniform average over this conformal manifold, with no RG-related complications (for recent discussions of averages over conformal manifolds see Maloney and Witten (2020); Afkhami-Jeddi et al. (2021), and for the marginal case see Berkooz et al. (2017)).

Surprisingly, we will find models where is negative at weak coupling. This signals a breakdown of the approximations involved in the computation, and so in this case the true chaos exponent simply vanishes, . In other words, we have

As a result, there are two possible behaviors for the onset of chaos: either the theory undergoes a continuous transition into chaos as in figure 1a or a discontinuous transition as in figure 1b, corresponding to whether is non-negative or negative at small enough respectively.2

The discontinuous transition into chaos is a surprising result, and it is tempting to compare it to similar results in classical chaos, the most famous one being the KAM theorem. In order to sharpen the comparison, we also discuss what a single core CFT should obey in order for the transition into chaos to be discontinuous. Similar works on the onset of quantum chaos include Stanford (2016); de Mello Koch et al. (2019); Chowdhury and Swingle (2017); Steinberg and Swingle (2019); Maldacena and Stanford (2016); Peng (2018), and Lian et al. (2019); Hu and Lian (2021) are especially relevant.

We will apply our formalism to two classes of examples where the disorder interaction is exactly marginal. The first class is disordered generalized free fields in d (following Gross and Rosenhaus (2017)) and in d. The second class is the disordered supersymmetric (SUSY) minimal models. In practice, we will only discuss the simplest case of the minimal model here. We will find a discontinuous transition in the former and a continuous transition in the latter.

More details and discussions on the computations and results can be found in the companion paper Berkooz et al. (2021).

Disorder around a nontrivial CFT

First, although the kernel is very complicated, knowing that an iterative ladder structure exists for the four-point function is already an important result since it allows for a systematic computation of , as we now discuss. The expansion in can also be used to determine whether the transition into chaos would be continuous or discontinuous (see figure 1). This requires finding the sign of in the limit . Using the leading contribution to in orders of (10), it is easy to see that the exponent is given by the maximal for which the integral (10) diverges. If the integral diverges at a positive (negative) value of , we have a continuous (discontinuous) transition into chaos.

However, we emphasize that it is not a chaos exponent in a single core CFT (as we take to be larger then any timescale of the core CFT); in fact, for unitary theories in it is always non-positive,  Caron-Huot (2017).

Surprisingly, under reasonable physical assumptions it can be shown that and are equal Berkooz et al. (2021). This amounts to showing that the integral (10) diverges for due to the large (negative) regime of the integrand. Putting these pieces together, we claim that satisfies

The LHS is calculated through the kernel equation in the limit , and the RHS is a property of the core CFT. We can interpret the result by noticing that describes the core CFT double-commutator behavior at large time scales. At arbitrarily weak coupling this behavior seems to control the behavior of the disordered theory double-commutator. The result is striking: in order to determine the type of transition into chaos, it is enough to find (the sign of) in a single core CFT. Below we give one example for each type of transition into chaos. In both cases we find that our conjecture (13) holds.

Examples of the Onset of chaos

Disordered generalized free fields

We now discuss our first class of examples with exactly marginal chaos, which are the disordered generalized free fields in d and in d. Generalized free fields (GFFs) are non-local theories with no energy-momentum tensor, but can be obtained by specific large-flavor limits of local theories, and are good toy-models for more complicated theories. The same analysis can be done for disordered GFFs in 2d. In this case we choose to work with SUSY GFFs, since this results in an exact conformal manifold even at finite . The model consists of generalized free chiral superfields of dimension , coupled via the superpotential

The computation is very similar, and the results appear in figure 4. At large enough , the chaos exponent for any approaches the result in the d SUSY versions of the SYK model Murugan et al. (2017); Bulycheva (2018). In addition, we again find that approaches as , and so for small enough is negative for any . As a result, we again find a discontinuous transition into chaos for any . We also find once again that the conjecture (13) is obeyed.

Disordered minimal models

We now discuss the disordered 2d minimal models. A single core CFT in this case consists of an SUSY minimal model, which can be represented by a single chiral superfield and superpotential . The full disordered theory is then

(19)

We emphasize that we interpret this equation in conformal perturbation theory in around copies of the minimal model, where is the chiral operator of dimension which appears in . Since the CFT at has no continuous non-R global symmetries, every classically marginal operator is exactly marginal Green et al. (2010); Kol (2002); Kol (2010), and so each deformation for is exactly marginal. Thus each realization of the model is conformal, and as a result averaged correlators of will also be conformal (even at finite ).

We can now attempt to compute in perturbation theory. This computation is generically difficult, and so we focus on the case , where a core CFT has central charge and so corresponds to the free compact boson at a specific radius. We can identify the operators in terms of vertex operators of the boson, and as a result we can read off all -point functions of the . Using this result to compute the leading contribution to the retarded kernel at small given in (10), we find that at small the exponent approaches zero. As a result, we expect a continuous transition into chaos in this model, as in figure 1a. In particular, the value of in a single minimal model is also zero, so that the conjecture (13) is again obeyed.
